rules.violation_condition: A non-SI legal unit is used for an audience that will not understand it, or in an international or jurisdictional context where the page’s additional acceptance conditions are not met.

5 tonnes
five t
five tonnes

tags.violation_condition: A number referring to a unit of measurement is written in words rather than numerals.

when: The number refers to a unit of measurement.
Applies whether the unit is a symbol or is spelled out.
rules.why: G-4: the heading, lead-in and ‘Always’ instruction state one numeral check; ‘Always’ supplies the hard modality.

anchor.quote: Use symbols for common units of measurement

covers.quote: After that, use the symbols.
Use symbols for units that are derived from time measurements, such as speed.

parts.quote: ‘mm’ for millimetres
‘cm’ for centimetres
‘km’ for kilometres
‘km/h’ for kilometres per hour
The speed limit for urban areas in NSW is 50 km/h.

tags.specification: Whether a unit is common and understood depends on the audience. Determining whether an unfamiliar unit has already been introduced can require the preceding document.
tags.violation_condition: A measurement unit is spelled out where the page calls for its symbol: for a common understood unit, after an unfamiliar unit has been introduced, or for a unit derived from time measurements.

when: Use symbols for well-known units users will understand.
After the first spelled-out use of an unfamiliar unit, use its symbol.
Use symbols for units derived from time measurements, such as speed.
The separate instruction requires ordinary days, years, hours and minutes to be spelled out, subject to its table, list and chart exception.
The separate sentence-start instruction requires a unit at the start of a sentence to be written in full.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: common units, subsequent mentions and time-derived units change when the same symbol-choice check applies.

anchor.quote: Spell out units of measurement the first time you use them if users won’t immediately understand them.

covers.quote: You don’t need to spell out units of measurement, even for the first use, if they’re well known and users will know what they mean.

parts.quote: The noise from the building site was 120 decibels (dB). Workers in the nearby office preferred a limit of only 50 dB.

tags.specification: The page gives no fixed inventory or audience test for units users will immediately understand.
tags.violation_condition: The first use of a unit that users will not immediately understand lacks its spelled-out name.

when: Applies at the first use of an unfamiliar unit.
Well-known units that users understand do not need to be spelled out, even on first use.
rules.why: G-3: the known-unit permission relaxes first-use expansion. This absence check is distinct from choosing symbols on later mentions.

anchor.quote: Don’t combine symbols and words for units.

parts.quote: Queensland is 1,853 million km2 in area.
Queensland is 1,853 million square km in area.

tags.violation_condition: A single unit expression mixes spelled-out unit components with symbols, as in ‘square km’.

when: Applies within the unit expression.
A scale word belonging to the number, such as ‘million’, is not itself a mixed unit component.
rules.why: G-1 and G-4: mixed components within a unit are a separate property from choosing a wholly spelled-out name or a symbol.

anchor.quote: Internationally accepted prefixes and their symbols make it easier for users to read, understand and compare numbers. Use them in government content.

examples.note: This is a correct equivalence, not a contrast marking the unprefixed quantity as wrong.

parts.quote: 63 megalitres is 63,000,000 litres

examples.note: This is a correct equivalence, not a contrast marking the unprefixed quantity as wrong.

parts.quote: 0.001 metre is 1 millimetre

tags.specification: The instruction concerns SI prefixes and their symbols. The page provides examples and a reference table but no magnitude threshold, preferred prefix or criterion for deciding when a prefixed form is required.
tags.violation_condition: A large or small measurement quantity lacks an appropriate internationally accepted prefix where the page calls for a prefixed expression.

when: Applies to large and small measurement quantities.
Data-storage and transfer prefixes follow the separately stated convention.
rules.why: G-4 and E-4: the body supplies the instruction absent from the descriptive heading; no unstated numerical threshold is invented.

anchor.quote: For this purpose, use:

covers.quote: The prefixes for data storage and transfer work differently to those used for SI units.
‘kilobyte’ for 1,000 B
‘megabyte’ for 1,024 kB
‘gigabyte’ for 1,024 MB
‘terabyte’ for 1,024 GB.

tags.violation_condition: A stated data-storage or transfer equivalence uses ‘kilobyte’, ‘megabyte’, ‘gigabyte’ or ‘terabyte’ with a factor different from the page’s specified mapping.

when: Applies when defining or converting quantities for data storage and transfer.
The page specifies kilobyte = 1,000 B, megabyte = 1,024 kB, gigabyte = 1,024 MB and terabyte = 1,024 GB.
rules.why: G-2: the four prefix mappings are lookup cases of one data-quantity convention, not four separate checks.

anchor.prefix: e time. These are not SI units.
anchor.quote: Spell them out in full – unless they’re in a table, list or chart and are easy to understand.

covers.quote: Days, years, hours and minutes measure time.
covers.suffix: These are not SI units. Spell t

parts.quote: I have been working in the public service for 12 years.
He started in the new department 20 days ago.
They sent the report in the last 15 minutes.

tags.specification: The referent is days, years, hours and minutes. Whether an abbreviation is easy to understand in a table, list or chart is audience-dependent and has no stated test.
tags.violation_condition: Days, years, hours or minutes are abbreviated outside an easily understood table, list or chart.

when: Applies to days, years, hours and minutes.
Abbreviations are allowed in tables, lists and charts when they are easy to understand.
Units derived from time measurements, such as speed, use symbols instead.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: time-unit abbreviation is one check with a format-and-understanding exception.

anchor.quote: Compare measurements using the same units

covers.quote: Use the same:
unit and prefix

parts.quote: The Green Wattle Creek fire burnt almost 3,000 km2, of which more than 1,000 km2 was national park.
The smaller jug held 1.5 L and the bigger jug held 2.0 L.
The piece of wood was 140 mm by 1,320 mm by 20 mm.
The Green Wattle Creek fire burnt almost 300,000 ha, of which more than 1,000 km2 was national park.
The smaller jug held 1,500 mL and the bigger jug held 2 L.
The piece of wood was 14 cm by 1.32 m by 20 mm.

tags.violation_condition: Measurements presented for comparison, including dimensions of one object, use inconsistent units or prefixes.

when: Applies to quantities presented for comparison.
Includes dimensions of the same object.
rules.why: G-4: the heading and first list item state one unit-consistency check; decimal-place consistency is independently flaggable.

anchor.quote: number of decimal places.

covers.quote: Use the same:

parts.quote: The smaller jug held 1.5 L and the bigger jug held 2.0 L.

examples.note: The same contrast also demonstrates inconsistent units and prefixes; in litres, the intended comparison is 1.5 L and 2.0 L.

parts.quote: The smaller jug held 1,500 mL and the bigger jug held 2 L.

tags.violation_condition: Quantities presented for comparison have inconsistent numbers of decimal places.

when: Applies to measurements presented for comparison.
Compare decimal precision after expressing the quantities using the same unit and prefix.
rules.why: G-1: decimal precision can be wrong even when units and prefixes match, so it is a separate check from unit consistency.

anchor.prefix: ntent and who will be using it.
anchor.quote: Most government content should use ‘L’ as it’s clearer to users (‘l’ can be confused with ‘I’ and ‘1’).

covers.quote: ‘litre’ can be represented as ‘L’ or ‘l’, depending on the type of content and who will be using it.

tags.specification: Prefer ‘L’ by default. Lowercase ‘l’ remains an accepted representation where the content type and audience make it appropriate; this is not an absolute ban.
tags.violation_condition: The lowercase litre symbol ‘l’ is used in ordinary government content where the clearer uppercase alternative ‘L’ is preferred.

when: Applies when litre is represented by a symbol.
The content type and intended users can justify lowercase ‘l’.
rules.why: G-3: the permission to use either symbol qualifies a named preference for ‘L’, rather than creating a second rule.

anchor.quote: Avoid imperial units

covers.quote: Don’t use imperial units of measurement in Australia unless you have a specific reason, such as:
in quotations from historical documents
when writing for readers in countries (particularly the United States) where imperial measures, or elements of them, still apply.

examples.note: An example in the discussion of contextual reasons, not an example labelled wrong.

parts.quote: gallons for volume of fuel

examples.note: An example in the discussion of contextual reasons, not an example labelled wrong.

parts.quote: barrels for volume of oil

examples.note: An example in the discussion of contextual reasons, not an example labelled wrong.

parts.quote: inches for the size of a screen

examples.note: An example in the discussion of contextual reasons, not an example labelled wrong.

parts.quote: feet for the altitude of a plane

tags.specification: The page gives examples of specific reasons but no exhaustive test. Audience, quotation status and conventional specialist use may require contextual review.
tags.violation_condition: Imperial measurements are used in Australian content without a specific contextual reason.

when: Applies to content for use in Australia.
Historical quotations can retain imperial units.
Imperial units can be appropriate for readers in countries where those measures remain in use.
The page also presents fuel gallons, oil barrels, screen inches and aircraft-altitude feet as examples in this exception discussion.
rules.why: G-2, G-3 and G-4: the body and exception list qualify one imperial-unit check rather than creating separate prohibitions or permissions.

anchor.quote: It’s good practice to also provide the equivalent quantity in SI units when that helps users.

parts.quote: In the 1970s, the speed limit for highways in many states of Australia was set at 60 miles per hour (97 km/h).

tags.specification: The page does not define when an SI equivalent would help users. This requires audience and context assessment rather than an unconditional conversion requirement.
tags.violation_condition: An imperial measurement lacks an equivalent SI quantity in a context where the conversion would help users.

when: An imperial measurement is retained for a specific reason.
Providing an SI equivalent would help the intended users.
rules.why: G-1: a missing helpful SI equivalent is distinct from unjustified use of imperial units.
